tagline: SSDI is insurance you already paid for. The claim is about proving the loss occurred while the policy was in force.

c.v: Social Security Disability Insurance is exactly what its name says: insurance. Every paycheck that had Social Security tax withheld paid a premium, and the policy pays a monthly benefit if you become unable to work before retirement age. In December 2025, 280,455 disabled Michigan workers were collecting on it, 54,205 of them in Wayne County, 23,615 in Macomb, 22,235 in Oakland, and 6,120 in Washtenaw, at an average of roughly $1,650 a month.
Because SSDI is insurance, the claim has two parts that other disability pages tend to blur. The first is

: were you insured when you became disabled? That depends on how recently you worked and, for many Michigan claimants who stopped working years before they applied, it is the question that decides the case. The second is
: are you disabled under the federal definition, and since when? The onset date determines not only whether you were covered but how much back pay you receive and when Medicare begins.

This page explains both. It covers the work-credit rules and the date last insured, how the benefit is calculated and what it pays in 2026, the five-month waiting period and retroactive benefits, Medicare, the benefits your family can draw on your record, how SSDI differs from SSI and from private disability insurance, what happens after approval, and what a Michigan SSDI lawyer does at each stage.

To receive SSDI, you must prove your disability began on or before your date last insured.

A Michigan worker who left the line in 2019 because of her back and applies in 2026 might have had a date last insured around December 2024, depending on her earnings record; her claim may depend on establishing that her disability began before that date, however disabled she is today. This is one important reason an otherwise strong SSDI claim can fail, and it is why the medical records from the years
the application matter as much as the current ones.

A progressive formula converts AIME to the primary insurance amount: 90 percent of the first portion, 32 percent of the next, and 15 percent above that, with the “bend points” between them adjusted each year. For workers first eligible in 2026, those bend points are $1,286 and $7,749.

faqs.question: How much is SSDI in Michigan?

answer.v: It depends on your earnings record, not on your condition or your state. The average Michigan disabled worker received about $1,650 a month in December 2025; the national average in January 2026 is $1,630; the 2026 maximum is $4,152. Your own estimate is on your Social Security Statement.

faqs.question: How many work credits do I need?

answer.v: Generally 20 credits in the ten years before you became disabled, plus enough total credits to be fully insured. Workers under 31 need fewer. In 2026 you earn one credit for each $1,890 in covered earnings, up to four a year.

faqs.question: I stopped working five years ago. Can I still get SSDI?

answer.v: Possibly, if you can prove your disability began before your date last insured, which for most workers falls about five years after the last full year of work. The medical records from that period are what matter. If the date has passed, SSI may be available instead.

faqs.question: What is the five-month waiting period?

answer.v: SSDI pays nothing for the first five full months after your established onset date. If your onset was more than five months before you applied, the wait has already run and payments begin on approval, with retroactive pay for up to 12 months before the application.
Twenty-four months after your first month of SSDI entitlement, and the back-pay months count. ALS and end-stage renal disease qualify immediately.

faqs.question: Can my family get benefits on my record?

answer.v: Yes: children under 18 (19 if in high school), a spouse caring for your child under 16, or a spouse 62 or older, each up to 50 percent of your benefit within the family maximum. They must be claimed.

faqs.question: Can I get SSDI and SSI at the same time?

answer.v: Yes, if your SSDI benefit is below the SSI payment standard ($994 in 2026) and your resources are under $2,000. SSI makes up the difference, less a $20 exclusion, and brings Medicaid.

faqs.question: Can I work while on SSDI?

answer.v: Yes, within the trial work period and extended period of eligibility rules. Nine months of unlimited earnings, then 36 months in which benefits are paid for months under $1,690. Report every month’s earnings.

faqs.question: Will SSDI reduce my long-term disability insurance?

answer.v: Usually. Most employer LTD policies require you to apply for SSDI and offset the LTD payment by the SSDI award, including back pay. Our long-term disability page explains the offset and the repayment demand that often follows an SSDI award.
Nothing unless you win, and then the lesser of 25 percent of your back pay or $9,200, approved and paid by Social Security. There is no fee on your ongoing benefits.
